imc-2025-01.title: Tangent lines through a given point
imc-2025-01.body:
Let $n=\deg P\ge2$ with leading coefficient $c\ne0$. The tangent line at $(r,P(r))$ is
$$\ell_r=\{(x,y):\ y=P(r)+P'(r)(x-r)\}.$$
So a point $(a,b)$ lies on $\ell_r$ if and only if $Q_{a}(r)=b$, where
$$Q_a(r)=P(r)+(a-r)P'(r).$$
The term of degree $n$ in $Q_a$ is $cr^n-r\cdot ncr^{n-1}=(1-n)cr^n$, and $(1-n)c\ne0$ since $n\ge2$. So $\deg Q_a=n$, with leading coefficient $(1-n)c$ independent of $a$.

**(a)** If $n$ is odd, then $Q_a(r)-b$ is a real polynomial of odd degree in $r$, hence has a real root $r$ (intermediate value theorem). Then $(a,b)\in\ell_r$. As $(a,b)$ was arbitrary, $\bigcup_r\ell_r=\mathbb R^2$. ∎

**(b) No.** If $n$ is even, fix any $a$. Then $Q_a$ is a polynomial of even degree with leading coefficient $(1-n)c\neq0$, so it is bounded above (if $(1-n)c<0$) or below (if $(1-n)c>0$) on $\mathbb R$. Say it is bounded above by $M$; then for $b>M$ the equation $Q_a(r)=b$ has no real solution, so $(a,b)$ lies on no tangent line (similarly in the other case with $b$ small). Hence the union is never all of $\mathbb R^2$.

**Answer to (b): No.** ∎

imc-2025-02.title: Cauchy–Schwarz with the weight $1-x^2$
imc-2025-02.body:
Let $g(x)=1-x^2$. Then $g(\pm1)=0$, $g'(1)=-2$, $g'(-1)=2$, $g''\equiv-2$. Integrating by parts twice,
$$\int_{-1}^1f''g\,dx=\Big[f'g\Big]_{-1}^1-\int_{-1}^1f'g'\,dx=0-\Big[fg'\Big]_{-1}^1+\int_{-1}^1fg''\,dx .$$
Here $[fg']_{-1}^1=f(1)g'(1)-f(-1)g'(-1)=-2-2=-4$ and $\int fg''=-2\int_{-1}^1f=0$. Hence $\int_{-1}^1f''g=4$.

Also $\int_{-1}^1g^2=\int_{-1}^1(1-2x^2+x^4)\,dx=2-\frac43+\frac25=\frac{16}{15}$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
$$16=\left(\int_{-1}^1f''g\right)^2\le\int_{-1}^1(f'')^2\cdot\int_{-1}^1g^2=\frac{16}{15}\int_{-1}^1(f'')^2,$$
so $\int_{-1}^1(f'')^2\ge15$.

**Equality.** Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz for continuous functions holds iff $f''=\lambda g$ on $[-1,1]$ for a constant $\lambda$. Then on $[-1,1]$
$$f(x)=\lambda\left(\frac{x^2}2-\frac{x^4}{12}\right)+\alpha x+\beta .$$
$\int_{-1}^1f=0$ gives $\lambda\left(\frac13-\frac1{30}\right)+2\beta=0$, i.e. $\beta=-\frac{3\lambda}{20}$. $f(1)=f(-1)$ gives $\alpha=0$, and $f(1)=1$ gives $\lambda\left(\frac12-\frac1{12}-\frac3{20}\right)=\frac{4\lambda}{15}=1$, so $\lambda=\frac{15}4$. Thus
$$f(x)=\frac{15}4\left(\frac{x^2}2-\frac{x^4}{12}\right)-\frac9{16}=\frac{-5x^4+30x^2-9}{16}\qquad(-1\le x\le1).$$
Conversely this function satisfies all conditions and $f''=\frac{15}4(1-x^2)$ gives $\int(f'')^2=\frac{225}{16}\cdot\frac{16}{15}=15$.

**Answer:** the minimum $15$ is attained exactly by the functions with $f(x)=\frac{-5x^4+30x^2-9}{16}$ on $[-1,1]$ (outside $[-1,1]$, $f$ can be any $C^2$ continuation). ∎

imc-2025-03.title: Describe $\mathcal S$, then compare $AB$ and $BA$
imc-2025-03.body:
**Answer: $\dfrac1{2^{2024}}$.** Let $n=2025$.

**The set $\mathcal S$.** Let $A=(a_{ij})\in\mathcal S$. Rank $1$ means all $2\times2$ minors vanish, so $a_{11}a_{ij}=a_{i1}a_{1j}=a_{i1}a_{j1}$ (symmetry), i.e. $a_{ij}=a_{11}a_{i1}a_{j1}$ as $a_{11}^2=1$. Put $u_i=a_{11}a_{i1}$; then $u_1=1$, $u_i\in\{\pm1\}$ and $u_iu_j=a_{i1}a_{j1}$, so $A=a_{11}\,uu^{\top}$. Conversely every $\pm uu^\top$ with $u\in\{\pm1\}^n$, $u_1=1$, is symmetric of rank $1$ with $\pm1$ entries, and the sign and $u$ are recovered from $A$ (as $a_{11}$ and $a_{11}$ times the first column). Hence $|\mathcal S|=2\cdot2^{n-1}=2^n$.

**Commuting.** Let $A=\sigma uu^\top$, $B=\tau vv^\top$ with $\sigma,\tau=\pm1$. Then
$$AB=\sigma\tau\,u(u^\top v)v^\top=\sigma\tau\langle u,v\rangle\,uv^\top,\qquad BA=\sigma\tau\langle u,v\rangle\,vu^\top.$$
$\langle u,v\rangle$ is a sum of $n=2025$ terms $\pm1$, an odd number, so it is nonzero. Thus $AB=BA\iff uv^\top=vu^\top$. The first column of $uv^\top$ is $v_1u=u$ and that of $vu^\top$ is $u_1v=v$; so $AB=BA$ forces $u=v$, and conversely $u=v$ gives equality. So $A,B$ commute iff $B=\pm A$.

For each $A$ there are exactly $2$ such $B$, so the probability is
$$\frac{2}{|\mathcal S|}=\frac2{2^{2025}}=\frac1{2^{2024}}.$$ ∎

imc-2025-04.title: Use $b=1$, then Bernoulli's inequality
imc-2025-04.body:
**Answer:** if $a=2$, then $x\in[-1,2)\cup[3,4)$; if $a\ge4$, then $x\in[-1,a)$.

Let $m=\lfloor x/a\rfloor$, so $am\le x<a(m+1)$. Since $a$ is even, the root requires $b^a+x\ge0$; for $b=1$ this gives $x\ge-1$, hence $m\ge-1$.

**Necessity ($b=1$).** (1) reads $\lfloor\sqrt[a]{1+x}\rfloor=1+m$, i.e. $(1+m)^a\le1+x<(2+m)^a$ (note $1+m\ge0$). Together with $am\le x<a(m+1)$, with $t=m+1\ge0$:
$$x\in\big[\max(a(t-1),\,t^a-1),\ \min(at,\,(t+1)^a-1)\big).\tag{2}$$
In particular $t^a-1<at$.
* For $t\ge2$ and $a\ge4$: $t^a-at-1=t(t^{a-1}-a)-1\ge2(2^{a-1}-a)-1>0$ because $2^{a-1}\ge a+1$ for $a\ge3$. Impossible.
* For $a=2$: $t^2-2t-1<0\iff t<1+\sqrt2$, so $t\le2$.

So $t\in\{0,1\}$, and also $t=2$ when $a=2$. By (2):
* $t=0$ ($m=-1$): $x\in[\max(-a,0-1),\min(0,0))=[-1,0)$;
* $t=1$ ($m=0$): $x\in[0,\min(a,2^a-1))=[0,a)$;
* $t=2$, $a=2$ ($m=1$): $x\in[\max(2,3),\min(4,8))=[3,4)$.

Hence $x\in[-1,a)$ for $a\ge4$, and $x\in[-1,2)\cup[3,4)$ for $a=2$.

**Sufficiency (all $b$).** Fix $b\ge1$ and put $u=b^{-a}\in(0,1]$. The left side of (1) is $y=b^{a-1}(b^a+x)^{1/a}=b^a(1+xu)^{1/a}\ge0$, and $N=b^a+m\ge0$. So (1) is equivalent to $N\le y<N+1$, i.e. (raising to the power $a$ and dividing by $b^{a^2}$)
$$(1+mu)^a\le1+xu<\big(1+(m+1)u\big)^a .$$
*Right inequality:* by Bernoulli, $(1+(m+1)u)^a\ge1+a(m+1)u>1+xu$, since $x<a(m+1)$ and $(m+1)u\ge0$.

*Left inequality:*
* $m=-1$ ($-1\le x<0$): $0\le1-u\le1$, so $(1-u)^a\le1-u\le1+xu$.
* $m=0$ ($0\le x<a$): $1\le1+xu$.
* $m=1$, $a=2$ ($3\le x<4$): $(1+u)^2=1+2u+u^2\le1+3u\le1+xu$ since $u\le1$.

So every $x$ in the stated sets satisfies (1) for all $b$. ∎

imc-2025-05.title: Cyclic part plus tails
imc-2025-05.body:
Fix $\tau\in T_n$. Let $C\subseteq[n]$ be the set of *cyclic* points ($\tau^k(x)=x$ for some $k\ge1$). $C$ is nonempty and $\tau$-invariant, and $\tau_c=\tau|_C$ is a permutation of $C$; let $N$ be its order (the lcm of its cycle lengths). Extending $\tau_c$ by the identity outside $C$ gives an element of $S_n$ of order $N$, so $N\le f(n)$.

For $x\notin C$ let $h(x)\ge1$ be the least $h$ with $\tau^h(x)\in C$; the points $x,\tau(x),\dots,\tau^{h(x)-1}(x)$ are distinct and outside $C$ (a repetition would make one of them cyclic). Let $R=\max_{x\notin C}h(x)$ ($R=0$ if $C=[n]$). For $k\ge R$ every $\tau^k(x)$ lies in $C$, hence $\tau^{k+N}=\tau^k$. So all powers of $\tau$ are among $\tau,\dots,\tau^{R+N}$ and
$$\operatorname{ord}(\tau)\le R+N .$$

**Case $R<n^{0.501}$.** Then $\operatorname{ord}(\tau)<f(n)+n^{0.501}$.

**Case $R\ge n^{0.501}$.** Then there are at least $R\ge n^{0.501}$ points outside $C$, so $|C|\le n-n^{0.501}$.

*Claim: some prime $p\le n^{0.501}$ divides none of the cycle lengths of $\tau_c$* (for $n$ large). Every integer $L\ge1$ is at least the sum of its distinct prime divisors (because $L\ge$ the product of these primes, and $xy\ge x+y$ for $x,y\ge2$). If every prime $p\le y:=n^{0.501}$ divided some cycle length, then
$$n\ge|C|=\sum_{\text{cycles}}L\ge\sum_{p\le y}p\ge1+2+\dots+\pi(y)\ge\frac{\pi(y)^2}2 .$$
By Chebyshev's estimate $\pi(y)\ge c\,y/\log y$ (for an absolute $c>0$), the right side is at least $\frac{c^2n^{1.002}}{2\,(0.501\log n)^2}$, which exceeds $n$ for large $n$ — contradiction.

Take such a $p$. As $p\le n^{0.501}\le n-|C|$, we can define $\tau_0\in S_n$ acting as $\tau_c$ on $C$, as a $p$-cycle on $p$ points outside $C$, and as the identity elsewhere. Since $p$ is prime and divides no cycle length, $p\nmid N$, so $\operatorname{ord}(\tau_0)=\operatorname{lcm}(N,p)=pN$. Hence $pN\le f(n)$ and $N\le f(n)/2$, so
$$\operatorname{ord}(\tau)\le N+R\le\frac{f(n)}2+n .$$
Finally $f(n)>2n$ for large $n$: with $k=\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor$, a permutation with disjoint cycles of the coprime lengths $k$ and $k+1$ has order $k(k+1)>2n$ once $n\ge12$. Hence $\frac{f(n)}2+n<f(n)$.

In both cases $\operatorname{ord}(\tau)<f(n)+n^{0.501}$ for all $\tau\in T_n$ when $n$ is large, i.e. $g(n)<f(n)+n^{0.501}$. ∎

imc-2025-06.title: Rolle's theorem for $(f(x)-k)/x$
imc-2025-06.body:
Define $\varphi(x)=\dfrac{f(x)-k}{x}$ on $[a,b]$. It is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $\varphi(a)=\varphi(b)=0$. By Rolle's theorem there is $\xi\in(a,b)$ with
$$0=\varphi'(\xi)=\frac{\xi f'(\xi)-(f(\xi)-k)}{\xi^2}.$$
Since $\xi>0$, this gives $f(\xi)-\xi f'(\xi)=k$. ∎

imc-2025-06.title: Cauchy's mean value theorem
imc-2025-06.body:
Let $g(x)=f(x)/x$ and $h(x)=1/x$ on $[a,b]$. Both are continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $h'(x)=-1/x^2\ne0$. By Cauchy's mean value theorem there is $\xi\in(a,b)$ with
$$\frac{g(a)-g(b)}{h(a)-h(b)}=\frac{g'(\xi)}{h'(\xi)}.$$
The left side is $\dfrac{k/a-k/b}{1/a-1/b}=k$. Since $g'(\xi)=\dfrac{\xi f'(\xi)-f(\xi)}{\xi^2}$ and $h'(\xi)=-\dfrac1{\xi^2}$, the right side is $f(\xi)-\xi f'(\xi)$. Hence $f(\xi)-\xi f'(\xi)=k$. ∎

imc-2025-07.title: Closure under addition, gcd, and gaps
imc-2025-07.body:
**Answer:** $M=\{md,(m+1)d,(m+2)d,\dots\}$ for some odd $d\ge1$ and some $m\ge1$.

**These work.** If $x=kd$ with $k\ge m$, then $2x=(2k)d\in M$. If $x=kd$, $y=ld$ ($k,l\ge m$) and $x+y=(k+l)d$ is even, then since $d$ is odd $k+l$ is even and $\frac{x+y}2=\frac{k+l}2d$ with $\frac{k+l}2\ge m$.

**Necessity.** Let $M$ satisfy (a), (b).

*1. $M$ is closed under addition:* for $x,y\in M$, $2x,2y\in M$ and $x+y=\frac{2x+2y}2\in M$.

*2. $M$ contains an odd number:* if $x\in M$ is even, then $x+2x=3x$ is even, so $\frac{3x}2\in M$ has a smaller power of $2$; repeat.

*3.* Let $d=\gcd(M)$; by step 2, $d$ is odd, and $M\subseteq d\mathbb Z_{>0}$. The gcd of $M$ is the gcd of finitely many elements $m_1,\dots,m_r$, so $d=\sum c_im_i$ with integers $c_i$. Let $P=\sum_{c_i>0}c_im_i$, $Q=\sum_{c_i<0}|c_i|m_i$. If $Q=0$ then $d\in M$ and $d,2d\in M$; otherwise $P,Q\in M$ by step 1 and $P-Q=d$. Either way **$M$ contains two elements differing by $d$.**

Let $c=\min M$. Recall that consecutive elements of $M$ differ by at least $d$.

*Claim A: if $a,a+d\in M$ and $a>c$, then $a-d\in M$.* Let $x$ be the largest element of $M$ below $a$. If $x+a$ were even, $\frac{x+a}2\in M$ would lie strictly between $x$ and $a$, impossible. So $x+a$ is odd and $x+a+d$ is even, so $z=\frac{x+a+d}2\in M$ with $x<z<a+d$. The only element of $M$ in $(x,a+d)$ is $a$, hence $z=a$, i.e. $x=a-d$.

*Claim B: if $a-d,a\in M$, then $a+d\in M$.* Let $x$ be the smallest element of $M$ above $a$ (it exists, as $2a\in M$). If $x+a$ were even, $\frac{x+a}2\in M$ would lie strictly between $a$ and $x$. So $x+a-d$ is even and $z=\frac{x+a-d}2\in M$ with $a-d<z<x$; the only element of $M$ there is $a$, so $x=a+d$.

Starting from a pair $a,a+d\in M$ and applying Claim A repeatedly we reach the pair $c,c+d\in M$ (the descent stops exactly at $c$, since $c$ is the minimum and all elements are $\equiv c\pmod d$). Then Claim B gives $c+kd\in M$ for all $k\ge0$. Conversely every element of $M$ is a multiple of $d$ and at least $c$, and $d\mid c$. Writing $c=md$: $M=\{kd:k\ge m\}$. ∎

imc-2025-08.title: Write the rotation as $JA^\top$
imc-2025-08.body:
**The rotation algebraically.** Rotating counter-clockwise moves the entry at $(i,j)$ to position $(n+1-j,i)$, i.e. $(A^{\mathsf R})_{ij}=A_{j,\,n+1-i}$ (check: $(A^{\mathsf R})_{12}=A_{2,3}=6$ in the example). Let $J$ be the reversal matrix, $J_{ik}=1$ if $k=n+1-i$ and $0$ otherwise. Then $(JA^\top)_{ij}=(A^\top)_{n+1-i,\,j}=A_{j,\,n+1-i}$, so
$$A^{\mathsf R}=JA^\top .$$
$J$ is real, symmetric and $J^2=I$.

**Consequence.** If $A=A^{\mathsf R}=JA^\top$, multiplying by $J$ gives $A^\top=JA$.

**Eigenvalues.** Let $Ax=\lambda x$, $x\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$. If $\lambda=0$ there is nothing to prove. Since $A$ is real, $A^*=A^\top$, and
$$|\lambda|^2\|x\|^2=\|Ax\|^2=x^*A^\top Ax=x^*JA(Ax)=\lambda\,x^*JAx=\lambda^2\,x^*Jx .$$
As $J$ is real symmetric (Hermitian), $x^*Jx$ is real. The left side is a positive real number, so $x^*Jx\ne0$ and $\lambda^2=\dfrac{|\lambda|^2\|x\|^2}{x^*Jx}$ is real. If $\lambda^2>0$ then $\lambda$ is real ($\operatorname{Im}\lambda=0$); if $\lambda^2<0$ then $\lambda$ is purely imaginary ($\operatorname{Re}\lambda=0$). ∎

imc-2025-09.title: Increments of the running maximum
imc-2025-09.body:
Let $Y_j=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_j\}$. Since $\mathbb E[Y_1]=\sum_ii2^{-i}=2=\frac{2}{2-1}$, it suffices to show $\mathbb E[Y_{j+1}-Y_j]=\frac{2^{j+1}}{2^{j+1}-1}$ for $1\le j\le n-1$.

**The probability of a sequence.** For distinct $c_1,\dots,c_{j+1}$, at step $t$ the rank of $c_t$ among the remaining integers is $c_t-\#\{s<t:c_s<c_t\}$. Hence
$$\mathbb P\big[(X_1,\dots,X_{j+1})=(c_1,\dots,c_{j+1})\big]=2^{-\sum c_t}\cdot2^{\#\{s<t:\ c_s<c_t\}}.$$
Group the outcomes by the set of values and the relative order of all values except the largest one. Inside a group only the position $i\in\{1,\dots,j+1\}$ of the largest value varies, and it contributes exactly $i-1$ pairs $s<t$ with $c_s<c_t$ (all elements before it), and none after. So inside each group the probabilities are proportional to $2^{i-1}$, and the largest value comes last with probability $\frac{2^j}{1+2+\dots+2^j}$. Therefore
$$\mathbb P[X_{j+1}>Y_j]=\frac{2^j}{2^{j+1}-1}.$$

**The overshoot.** Condition on $X_1,\dots,X_j$, with maximum $Y_j$. Exactly $r=Y_j-j$ remaining integers are below $Y_j$, so $Y_j+t$ has rank $r+t$ among the remaining ones ($t\ge1$). Hence
$$\mathbb E\big[(X_{j+1}-Y_j)\mathbf 1_{X_{j+1}>Y_j}\,\big|\,X_1,\dots,X_j\big]=\sum_{t\ge1}t\,2^{-r-t}=2\cdot2^{-r}=2\,\mathbb P\big[X_{j+1}>Y_j\,\big|\,X_1,\dots,X_j\big].$$
Since $Y_{j+1}-Y_j=(X_{j+1}-Y_j)\mathbf 1_{X_{j+1}>Y_j}$, taking expectations gives
$$\mathbb E[Y_{j+1}-Y_j]=2\,\mathbb P[X_{j+1}>Y_j]=\frac{2^{j+1}}{2^{j+1}-1}.$$
Summing, $\mathbb E[Y_n]=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{2^i}{2^i-1}$. ∎

imc-2025-09.title: Tail sums and telescoping
imc-2025-09.body:
For an integer $k\ge1$, given that $X_1,\dots,X_{i-1}$ are all $<k$, exactly $k-i$ integers below $k$ remain and they have ranks $1,\dots,k-i$; so $\mathbb P[X_i<k\mid X_1,\dots,X_{i-1}<k]=1-2^{-(k-i)}$ (which is $0$ if $k\le i$, correctly). Hence with
$$P_n(k)=\prod_{i=1}^n\left(1-2^{i-k}\right),\qquad \mathbb E[Y_n]=\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbb P[Y_n\ge k]=\sum_{k\ge1}\big(1-P_n(k)\big).$$
We show by induction that this equals $\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{2^i}{2^i-1}$. For $n=1$: $\sum_k2^{1-k}=2$. For $n\ge2$ it suffices that
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\big(P_{n-1}(k)-P_n(k)\big)=\sum_{k\ge1}2^{n-k}P_{n-1}(k)=\frac{1}{1-2^{-n}} .$$
Now $P_n(k+1)=(1-2^{-k})P_{n-1}(k)$ and $P_n(k)=(1-2^{n-k})P_{n-1}(k)$, so
$$(1-2^{-n})\,2^{n-k}P_{n-1}(k)=(2^{n-k}-2^{-k})P_{n-1}(k)=P_n(k+1)-P_n(k).$$
Summing over $1\le k\le K$ telescopes to $P_n(K+1)-P_n(1)=P_n(K+1)\to1$ as $K\to\infty$ (note $P_n(1)=0$). This proves the identity and hence the formula. ∎

imc-2025-10.title: Group by square-free part; non-fundamental Pell solutions are rare
imc-2025-10.body:
**Answer: the limit is $1$** (essentially only the trivial pairs $a=b$ count).

**Reformulation.** For $a\ge1$ write $a(a+1)=d_az^2$ with $d_a$ square-free. A product of two positive integers is a square iff they have the same square-free part, so $(a^2+a)(b^2+b)$ is a square iff $d_a=d_b$. With $c_d=\#\{a\le N:d_a=d\}$ we get $\sum_dc_d=N$ and
$$S_N=\sum_dc_d^2=N+\sum_dc_d(c_d-1).$$
It remains to show $E_N:=\sum_dc_d(c_d-1)=o(N)$.

**Pell equations.** Since $a^2<a^2+a<(a+1)^2$, $a(a+1)$ is not a square, so $d=d_a\ge2$ is not a square. Multiplying by $4$: $(2a+1)^2-d(2z)^2=1$. So every $a$ with $d_a=d$ gives a positive solution $(x,y)=(2a+1,2z)$ of $x^2-dy^2=1$ with $x\le2N+1$, and different $a$ give different solutions. By the theory of Pell's equation, the positive solutions are $x_k+y_k\sqrt d=\varepsilon^k$ ($k\ge1$), where $\varepsilon=x_1+y_1\sqrt d>2$ is the fundamental solution, and $x_k=\frac{\varepsilon^k+\varepsilon^{-k}}2\ge\frac{\varepsilon^k}2$. Let $K_d$ be the number of $k$ with $x_k\le2N+1$ and $T_d=\max(K_d-1,0)$ the number of such $k\ge2$. Then $c_d\le K_d\le\log_2(4N+2)=:L$ and
$$c_d(c_d-1)\le K_d(K_d-1)\le L\,T_d,\qquad\text{so}\qquad E_N\le L\sum_dT_d .$$

**Counting non-fundamental solutions.** If $k\ge2$, pick a prime $p\mid k$ and let $u+v\sqrt d=\varepsilon^{k/p}$ (a positive solution, so $u\ge2$). Then
$$x_k=\frac{(u+v\sqrt d)^p+(u-v\sqrt d)^p}2=\sum_{j\text{ even}}\binom pj u^{p-j}(v\sqrt d)^j\ \ge u^p ,$$
and $x_k$ is determined by $(u,p)$. Also each value $x$ determines $d$ (the square-free part of $x^2-1$) and then $k$. Hence $\sum_dT_d$ is at most the number of pairs $(u,p)$ with $u\ge2$, $p$ prime, $u^p\le X:=2N+1$. For each $p$ there are at most $X^{1/p}$ values of $u$, and $p\le\log_2X$, so
$$\sum_dT_d\le X^{1/2}+X^{1/3}\log_2X=O(\sqrt N).$$
Therefore $E_N=O(\sqrt N\log N)=o(N)$, and
$$\frac{S_N}N=1+\frac{E_N}N\longrightarrow1.$$ ∎

*Remark.* Non-trivial pairs do exist, e.g. $a=4b(b+1)$: then $a(a+1)=4b(b+1)(2b+1)^2$, which has the same square-free part as $b(b+1)$. They are only about $\sqrt N$ in number, consistent with the bound above.
